questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: For me, it was important to improve language skills/have some pre-existing knowledge of the language being spoken in the host country, and due to having studied French in school but never having had the opportunity to use it, I chose France. It was equally important to me to study in a place that was international, cosmopolitan and offered many opportunities academically.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Once I had received my Login data for the student portal and email of the host university, this was very easy, as all information was provided by email.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The first week in the study destination I participated in an introduction week and there was introduction event for all exchange students as well. I did not receive any direct assistance, but always felt that I could ask questions at these events when needed.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: One day of the introduction course as well as an introduction cocktail didn't take place as planned due to the strikes happening in France at that time (the cocktail was later moved to another date, where I unfortunately could not make it). But it feels unfair to include these "force majeure" events in the overall judgement.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I was offered Crous housing through my university, but actually ended up deciding against it as I was offered a room in the Cité Universitaire, which I was very satisfied with. So I was in the lucky position of being able to choose, which of course is a more positive experience than many other students, and I can't speak to the quota of exchange students that get offered a room at Crous.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Paris is an expensive city, but the Cité Internationale Universitaire de Paris (CIUP) isn't just a great place to live, but also often cheaper. So it is definitely worth it to apply to either a house representing your country of origin or through the general portal.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I can't speak to the Crous residence I was offered initially, but the experience living at CIUP was wonderful, and I spoke to many friends who were satisfied with their Crous housing, especially since it's cheap compared to renting a studio/room (though not always easy to come by).

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The registration form was very much tailored to French students, so there were some parts that were hard to parse or answer from an international background (for example, having to choose a category for my parents' employment or which French grade my non-French secondary school qualification amounts to). But it was manageable.
The bigger issue was the Learning Agreement - the problems that I faced were more due to the requirements of my home university not matching up with the information available from the host university, but it was still a very frustrating and stressful experience. I needed to get courses pre-approved at my home university by the end of October so I could have a signed Learning Agreement for applying to the host university. For this pre-approval, I needed in-depth information about courses including literature or at least a description. This, I was informed, was usually only available by the start of January. So I had to choose courses for my Learning Agreement based on which courses I could find information on (through the course catalogue or mailing professors and teachers), knowing that I would want to change these later and go through the process again.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Once I had a signed Learning Agreement, I had to upload this and other documents in a portal the details of which I don't remember, but it was quite easy. A few weeks later, in late November, I was emailed the first login data to use to activate my student account and email.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I mailed a few questions and my concerns about the lack of course information in August to the Erasmus responsible; I didn't receive a reply, which makes sense now that I know that universities are basically on holiday in August in France. I did receive answers from several professors, and also had the email addresses of both the university's and my department's international contacts.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Since my first learning agreement was based on which courses I had information on and could pre-approve, I had to make changes to my learning agreement once I had information on the courses I wanted to attend. I was succesful in this and luckily my home university sped up the pre-approval process for me since I was already abroad. The only frustration arose when the Erasmus responsible at the host university seemed to be unacquainted with the PDF format of the online learning agreement that my home university used and contacted me thinking I had signed up for non-existing courses. I needed to tell her to scroll down in the document to actually see the changes I made to the learning agreement in a second table that was attached, which she apparently hadn't done and which was a little frustrating after all the work and time I had spend on the whole process.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Course information and literature is often not available until shortly before the semester starts. However, many of the professors are very friendly responsive and courses repeat, so reaching out to them asking about course content / descriptions from previous semesters is definitely worth it and a good way to establish "first contact".

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The courses I took were definitely interesting. It is worth noting that in the spring semester, M1 students in political science have to write their "Mémoire", which can be compared with a small master's thesis. All courses were thus only planned for eight weeks and supposed to end by the end of March. This changed due to the strikes and classes being cancelled, but the max amount of course days was still only eight, which of course is short compared to a 12/13 week semester i Denmark. This only applies to Political Science in the spring, though, and the professors were quite flexible with their deadlines (so that not all exams/deadlines were directly after courses ended).

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The courses were challenging and the teachers were very competent. I often felt challenged in a good way and learned a lot.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The French way of teaching, as is also known about French school in general, is very much more authoritarian and less lax than in Denmark. In one of my first courses, the teacher would scold every student that was late and even pretended to hit one on the head with a roll of paper, which felt like a return to school. On the upside of this more "frontal" way of teaching was that the teachers would often start talking about a topic, without any notes, and make a brilliant explanation of a certain topic. Since another big difference was the lack of powerpoints or detailed notes about every session (only some teachers did limited versions of this which do not compare to the amount of material usually uploaded by teachers in Denmark), to get something out of the course, it was required to take notes fast while the teachers were talking. This could get quite stressful in combination with the courses being three hours long with only a short break in the middle. This also meant, though, that every attendance led to thousands of words of useful notes.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- Interventions internationales de gestion des crises
- Migrations, diasporas et réfugiés
- Décider dans un monde incertain
- Administrations européennes
- Fabrique de l'autorité politique

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Personally I got the most out of the courses Interventions internationales de gestion des crises, administrations européennes and Fabrique de l'autorité. The teachers were very competent and added to this, these courses were only attended by students from one to two master programmes and were thus real courses in course room were you were able to contribute, as opposed to big lectures.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: A lot of museums are free for students and/or people up to 25 years of age (or everyone, such as Carnevalet). However, this doesn't apply to temporary exhibitions, which can cost around 13€. Other than that, I did not encounter any unexpected costs so much as costs due to the spontaneous nature of Erasmus life including a lot of going out, concerts, et cetera.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
The cost of living due to inflation was quite high. Eating and drinking when going out I had expected to be cheaper than in Copenhagen, and they were, but not as much as I had thought. Paris is still an expensive city. 
However, the Crous canteen was a life saviour. There is one at CIUP, but also in other places (I heard there is one on a boat on the Seine though I haven't been there myself), and a meal including a salad, fruit and/or yoghurt cost 3,30€. The vegetarian option was almost always tasty. I knew a lot of people who would eat lunch and/or dinner there every day. Coffee and cake the other hours of the day are also cheap and there is a reduced price option for students.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: It was possible to book a sports course through the university, which you had to attend throughout the semester and got graded on. I did not expect that there would be a requirement of attendance and several obligatory tests, but it was still fun. There were always events happening at the university, though not that many clubs as I had expected (or they were hard to find as an international student / less active due to the strikes). There was also a volunteer organisation offering events for exchange students and a WhatsApp group, though unfortunately most events took place in the start of the semester and then it died down completely, which I assume might be due to a lack of volunteers.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I booked a sports membership at CIUP where I lived, which cost only 80€ for a whole semester. I attended many different events - in Paris, there is always something happening, and there are always other exchange students planning something or events for exchange students. I wish I had attended more cultural offers at the university itself, but the talk and cinema events I did attend were great. As stated above, I can imagine that there is quite a bit more activity from student clubs in other semesters where there isn't a national strike going on almost every week.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Paris offers so many great museums and experiences it is dazzling. Since I regret not doing this more, I recommend taking weekends and free days to take trips out of the city, since these are the places that you are less likely to go to when you are back in Paris and have limited time. I went, for example, to Étretat in Normandy, Versailles, Givergny including Claude Monet's garden, and Fontainebleau, and they were all great experiences.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The main difference was the hectic pace of Paris as a big world city with millions of people, compared to Copenhagen which is a lot smaller and more quiet. The teaching style as stated above also took some getting used to, but there were always other international students to make courses less daunting and to talk to about these experiences. So it didn't take long for me to adjust.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Socialising with local students was borderline impossible given how busy they were due to the mixed pressure of the courses I also attended and the important mémoire coming up. So I don't have any tips in that direction, unfortunately.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The more authoritarian teaching style as mentioned above was probably one of the most challenging things since it could be intimidating. Other than that, I had heard many horror stories about rude Parisians, but actually had many extremely friendly interactions with French strangers. I found that people often were more open and easier to talk to than Danes, who can be quite closed off and shy despite being friendly.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: All the clichéd ideas about Paris are true; there is a wonderful joie de vivre in the city, it is full of culture, good food and drink, and secret places to discover. I loved doing things spontaneously, going out, and enjoying the energy of the city. It is truly a great place to live for half a year.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: That the course selection process can be quite frustrating and that patience is required (and contacting professors if necessary), that the Master's level courses are very rewarding especially if you select the ones that are attended by a smaller number of students, and that there are always a handful of other Erasmus students attending the same courses, at least in my experience, so you normally aren't alone.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The phase before applying to the host university (getting the Learning Agreement signed, courses pre-approved and so on) can be extremely stressful, but once that is done, everything is much easier.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: For me it was being able to study in the old Sorbonne building in the middle of the inner city and truly feeling challenged by the courses. Also making a lot of friends and establishing international contacts.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: During the exchange, it was probably the abrupt changes being caused by the strikes, and not knowing whether a building might be closed, whether a course would take place at uni, online or not at all, et cetera. Since many courses were repeated, it wasn't the academic consequences so much as the insecurity about what was going to happen that could be stressful. Of course, this was ultimately out of anyone's control.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
